title: Evidence Prioritization
summary: Teach the reviewer to evaluate the quality and importance of evidence rather than simply counting pieces of evidence.
learningObjectives: Recognize when multiple sources reinforce the same reading.
Recognize when conflicting evidence weakens the reading.
Build findings around the strongest available support.

definitions.primaryEvidence: The strongest evidence supporting a finding.
definitions.secondaryEvidence: Evidence that reinforces but does not independently establish the finding.
definitions.multipleEvidenceSources: Independent clues that point to the same conclusion.
definitions.conflictingEvidence: Evidence that pushes the reviewer toward a weaker conclusion or review-only outcome.

reviewerPrinciples: Direct evidence has higher value than inference.
Multiple independent sources can outrank a single weak cue.
Conflicting evidence must be resolved before the finding is finalized.
Findings should cite the strongest supporting evidence.
reviewerQuestions: Does weaker evidence merely reinforce the strongest evidence?
Does the strongest evidence still hold after conflict is considered?
Would another reviewer choose the same primary evidence?

examples.text: The character openly threatens another character.
Several characters imply a threat but none state it.
One witness points to bribery and the next scene confirms the exchange.

counterExamples.text: Five weak hints outweigh one direct confession.
Ignore a strong direct cue because a weaker cue appears first.
counterExamples.reason: Ordering is not the same as priority.

commonMistakes: Counting evidence instead of evaluating it.
Treating multiple weak clues as equivalent to one strong clue.

questions.question: Is one strong piece of evidence usually better than many weak ones?
Should findings cite the strongest evidence available?
Can speculative evidence become primary evidence?
